===== ORIGINAL PROMPT (initial_prompt.md) =====
Design and build a complex, production-shaped native iOS app that requires a
real server-side backend (not local-only, not a static/offline app) — pick a
genuinely creative, non-obvious idea that solves a real, specific pain point
well enough that it has a real shot at organic/viral growth. Do not default
to another todo-list, habit-tracker, journaling, or AI-wrapper app — those
categories are saturated and none of them are "unique." Think harder for an
underserved, emotionally sticky, inherently-social-or-real-time problem
where a mobile client + backend architecture is actually necessary (real-time
sync across users/devices, a shared/live data feed, matching or coordination
between people, server-side processing too heavy for on-device, etc.) — the
backend requirement should come from the idea being genuinely multi-user or
real-time, not be bolted on.

Requirements for the idea itself (spend real effort on this — the idea is
the deliverable, not just the code):
- Solves one specific, sharply-defined pain point for a specific audience
  (not "everyone"). Be able to state the pain point and audience in one
  sentence each.
- Has a natural viral/sharing loop baked into the core mechanic — not a
  bolted-on "invite friends" button, but something where using the app is
  inherently more valuable or fun with other people, or naturally produces
  something worth sharing outside the app.
- Genuinely requires a backend: real-time multiplayer/sync, a live shared
  feed, server-side matching/aggregation, push notifications driven by
  server-side events, or similar — justify the architecture choice.
- Is creative enough that a stranger hearing the one-line pitch would say
  "oh that's clever" rather than "isn't that just [existing app]?"

Technical scope:
- Native iOS client (SwiftUI).
- A real backend service (your choice of stack — pick something sensible
  and justify it) handling auth, data sync/storage, and whatever real-time
  or server-side logic the concept needs.
- Design the API contract, data model, and sync/real-time strategy properly
  before building — this is a "complicated app," not an MVP toy.
- Production-shaped: reasonable auth flow, error handling, loading/empty/
  offline states, and a coherent onboarding funnel a real user could follow.
- Visual design should be distinctive and match the concept — not generic
  default SwiftUI styling — but the primary bar for this app is the idea,
  the architecture, and it actually working end-to-end (client <-> backend).

Start by proposing and committing to the specific concept (pain point,
audience, viral loop, and why it needs a backend) before moving into specs
and build, and carry that concept consistently through naming, design, and
onboarding copy.

**Codex (Product Strategist · User Advocate) — Round 1**

One-sentence product promise: Pulse Relay lets a parent in a school-pickup pod broadcast an urgent same-day pickup replacement request and get one trusted pod member to lock it in in real time, with no confusion over who is actually covering it.

Primary user and scenario: a parent/guardian of a child under 13 in a known classroom/community pod who hits an unexpected pickup disruption (traffic, illness, forgotten drop-off plans) and needs to coordinate a safe handoff fast from a mobile phone while at home, in traffic, or at a school exit point.

Core loop: post a relay request into the pod, wait for pod members to see a live request stream and accept actions, resolve acceptance as a server-enforced first-accept-wins event so everyone sees exactly one confirmed coverer or a clean already-claimed state, then complete the handoff and generate a privacy-safe relay receipt log that can be shared externally as proof of coverage.

Hard scope boundaries: one app only, not two apps; school-pickup pod type only (no daycare/activity variants); no GPS/live location or maps in v1; no child names/photos/face data in requests; matching only through explicit trust-graph/pod membership via invite link or admin pod code (never open stranger matching); no “verified/background-checked” claims that are not actually performed; no assumed cold-start at classroom scale solve attempt—onboarding friction reduction only; and no mock or placeholder data shown as real user content.

Measurable success criteria: backend reachability is proven from iOS before feature validation is accepted; every stateful screen renders real loading/empty/error/success paths; two separate real pod accounts can successfully race acceptance on the same request with exactly one winner and one explicit already-claimed loser; accepted/completed states are only shown after server acknowledgment; a zero-state user can join or create via pod code/link without dead-ending; and forced-quit/relaunch preserves auth session and relevant feed state.

Biggest objection to guard against is trust drift: if the app lets users infer background checks or identity guarantees it does not provide, parents will lose trust fast. The detail that must be preserved end-to-end is this “pod + one-server lock + dual-purpose relay receipt/audit artifact” core, not any secondary feature.

**Claude (Design Lead · Systems Thinker) — Round 1**

Here's my take, coming at this from the screens-and-flows side rather than the concept side, since I think the concept is solid but nobody's yet forced it through an actual information architecture and that's where the real gaps will show up.

Product promise, stated the way I'd want a developer to say it back to me: pulse-relay lets a parent in a specific school pickup pod broadcast "I can't make pickup today" to the small group of people who already know and trust each other, and guarantees that exactly one of them locks it in, with no ambiguity about who's actually coming. The primary user and scenario is not abstract — it's a parent standing somewhere stressed at 2:30-2:45pm on a weekday, phone in one hand, who has maybe ninety seconds of attention to give this app before they either get an answer or go back to texting the class group chat as a fallback. That framing matters for IA: every screen in the core path has to be legible in a glance, one-handed, under stress. If any screen in the post-request or accept path requires reading a paragraph or making more than one real decision, we've already lost against the group chat.

Core loop as I'd actually build the screens: open app → pod home shows either "nothing pending" (true empty state, not a blank screen) or the current open request if one exists → if you need help, one big affordance to post a same-day request with a time window and optional short note → that request appears live for other pod members, who get a push notification that deep-links straight into the request card, not into a generic inbox → tap accept → optimistic "you've got it" state on the accepter's device while the server arbitrates → server confirms first-accept-wins, that device shows confirmed, everyone else's device (including any other pod member who tapped accept a beat later) shows "already covered by [pod member]" with zero ambiguity → requester's screen updates to show who's got it → either side marks it complete → that generates one record that's simultaneously the audit log entry and the shareable receipt card.

The part I don't think has been fully reasoned through yet, and where I want to plant a flag as the systems-thinking pass: what happens off the happy path. Three cases the IA has to actually account for, not hand-wave: first, an accepted request where the accepter later can't follow through — if there's no "back out" path, the first person to bail traps the requester with a false sense of security, which is worse than no acceptance at all, so there needs to be an explicit "I can no longer cover this" action that reopens the request and re-notifies the pod, distinct from a fresh post. Second, an unfulfilled request — nobody accepts within some window — needs its own visible state (not an infinite spinner or silent nothing) so the requester knows to escalate outside the app; I'd say something like a visible "still open" indicator plus maybe a gentle re-broadcast affordance, since silence reading as "handled" is exactly the kind of false confidence that makes an app in this category actively dangerous rather than just useless. Third, two unrelated requests open in the same pod at once (two different families both have a same-day conflict) — the feed and notifications need to disambiguate cleanly per-child-generic-reference and per-requester, or you get exactly the confusion this app exists to prevent.

One more IA-level decision I want locked now rather than discovered mid-build: who can create a pod versus who can only join one. Somebody has to be able to mint an invite link or join code, which means there's a lightweight admin/creator role even though we're deliberately not building a "pod management" screen suite — I'd keep this to the minimum viable action (create pod → get a code/link → done) rather than a full admin console, consistent with the earlier call that secondary screens get cut before core-loop fidelity does.

Hard scope boundaries I want stated explicitly so nobody quietly re-adds them under time pressure: no in-app chat/messaging thread (the request card plus a single optional short note is the entire communication surface — if people need to negotiate, that's a sign the request needs to be reposted, not a sign we need DMs), no location or map view anywhere, no child names/photos/PII, no daycare or activity pod types, no recurring/scheduled requests (same-day only), no payments. And one I'd add that isn't in the prior decisions yet: no persistent request history feed beyond what's needed for the receipt/audit record — this isn't a social feed you scroll, it's a single current-state screen.

Measurable success criteria, the kind that can actually be checked rather than eyeballed: the two-device race test (both devices tap accept within the same second) must resolve to exactly one confirmed acceptor and one explicit "already claimed" rejection, every time, not most of the time; time from request post to push notification landing on a second real device should be verified in practice, not assumed, with a target under a minute; every screen in both core funnels — post-request and accept/resolve/complete — must have real empty, loading, error, and success states, checkable by pulling network access mid-flow; a fresh account with no pod must be able to reach a working join-or-create path with zero dead ends; and the whole loop must be run start-to-finish with two genuinely separate seeded accounts in the same pod, not one account and a mocked second party.

My biggest objection to my own framing: I've designed this assuming a single active request at a time is the common case, and if pods turn out to routinely have multiple overlapping requests, the "glanceable single card" IA breaks down into something that needs a real list/queue with its own empty/loading states — I think that's fine to defer, but the data model shouldn't assume single-active-request as a hard constraint even if the UI optimizes for it.
